C-HLB is a within-group whole-brain contrast of a WCST variant (task C) vs baseline and reflects executive processes (matching and instructed set-shifting); meets pooled executive-function criteria.
C-HLB isolates matching and instructed set-shifting with minimal working-memory demand; it does not specifically reflect memory load/maintenance/manipulation required by WORKING_MEMORY_I2.
The contrast is not an inhibition paradigm (e.g., Go/No-Go, Stroop); it isolates matching/set-shifting rather than inhibitory control.
Task C involves instructed set-shifting relative to no set-shifting (C-HLB), so the contrast reflects switching/set-shifting demand (WCST variant).
This contrast does not use a planning paradigm (Tower tasks) and does not isolate planning demands.
Contrast is not a vigilance/oddball paradigm nor a target-detection main effect; it isolates matching and set-shifting instead.
This is not an initiation/word-generation paradigm and does not reflect self-initiated generation.

B-HLB is a within-group whole-brain contrast of WCST variant B vs baseline and reflects executive processes (instructed set changes and simple working memory); meets pooled executive-function criteria.
Authors state B-HLB additionally involves simple working-memory operations (maintenance/retrieval); the contrast reflects working-memory demand (simple WM) consistent with WORKING_MEMORY_I2.
B-HLB is not an inhibition paradigm (e.g., Go/No-Go, Stroop) and does not isolate inhibitory demand.
B-HLB contrasts instructed set-shifting (B) vs no set-shifting (HLB) and thus reflects switching/set-shifting demand within the WCST framework.
This contrast does not employ a planning paradigm (Tower tasks) and does not isolate planning demands.
B-HLB is not an oddball/vigilance target-detection contrast and does not specifically index set-maintenance under interference as required by VIGILANCE_I1/I2.
This is not a word-generation/initiation paradigm and does not reflect self-initiated generation.
A-HLB is a within-group whole-brain WCST main-effect contrast reflecting multiple executive demands (complex working memory, set-shifting, error processing); meets pooled executive-function criteria.
A-HLB engages complex/manipulative working-memory operations (authors report DLPFC involvement and working-memory manipulation), satisfying WORKING_MEMORY_I2.
A-HLB is not a canonical inhibition contrast (Go/No-Go, Stroop); inhibitory demand is not the primary isolated process.
A-HLB includes uninstructed set-shifting operations as part of the full WCST contrast (set-shifting vs baseline), meeting cognitive-flexibility criteria.
Although A involves complex executive processes, it is not a Tower planning paradigm and does not isolate planning in the sense required by PLANNING_I1.
A-HLB is not an oddball/vigilance target-detection contrast; vigilance criteria are not met.
This contrast does not involve word-generation/initiation paradigms and does not index self-initiated generation.

The conjunction of (A-HLB)*(B-HLB)*(C-HLB) identifies a common frontoparietal network across WCST variants; this is a within-group whole-brain executive-task conjunction and meets pooled executive-function criteria.

The conjunction identifies common activations across tasks (general matching/control network) but does not specifically isolate memory-load, maintenance, or manipulation (WORKING_MEMORY_I2 not clearly met).
The conjunction is not an inhibition paradigm contrast and does not isolate inhibitory demand.

Although the tasks are WCST variants, the conjunction is a common main-effect map (task vs baseline) and does not specifically isolate switching/switch>repeat or set-shifting demand required by COGNITIVE_FLEXIBILITY_I2.
Conjunction does not use a planning (Tower) paradigm and does not isolate planning demand.
The conjunction is not an oddball/vigilance target-detection contrast and does not isolate set-maintenance under interference.
This conjunction does not involve word-generation/initiation paradigms and does not index self-initiated generation.

A–C is a within-group whole-brain contrast isolating the cognitive gradient in WCST (error detection, complex WM, uninstructed set-shifting) and therefore reflects pooled executive-function processes.
Authors report A–C reveals complex working-memory operations and manipulative WM demands (DLPFC), so the contrast reflects working-memory manipulation consistent with WORKING_MEMORY_I2.
A–C contrasts cognitive gradient/set-shifting and error processing; it is not a canonical inhibition paradigm isolating inhibitory control.
A–C contrasts the most complex (A) with the simplest (C) WCST variants and captures uninstructed vs instructed switching and set-shifting demands, meeting cognitive-flexibility criteria.
Although A–C indexes complex executive processing, it is not a Tower planning paradigm and does not specifically isolate planning as defined by PLANNING_I1.
A–C is not an oddball/vigilance target-detection contrast; it isolates shifting/error/WM components rather than vigilance per se.
This contrast does not involve word-generation/initiation tasks and does not index initiation.
A–B isolates differences between uninstructed and instructed WCST variants (error detection, set-shifting) in a within-group whole-brain contrast, representing executive-function processes.
A–B primarily highlights error detection/feedback utilization and uninstructed vs instructed set-shifting (type II activations) rather than isolating working-memory load/manipulation specifically.
A–B is not a canonical inhibition contrast and does not isolate inhibitory control processes (e.g., No-Go>Go).

B−A (visual control vs motor control) is a within-group, whole-brain task contrast that engages selective attention/vigilance and anterior cingulate, fitting the pooled executive-function category.
The visual control task is a perceptual/attention discrimination, not a canonical working-memory paradigm; it does not meet WORKING_MEMORY_I1.
This contrast does not involve an inhibition paradigm (e.g., Go/No-Go, Stroop); it isolates a different executive domain.
The contrast is not a task-switching/set-shifting paradigm and does not probe switching demands.
The visual discrimination/motor control contrast does not involve Tower-type planning operations.
The visual-control task requires maintaining a discrimination set and detecting the side with more dead-ends (sustained/target-like attention), fitting vigilance criteria.
This contrast does not test self-initiated generation (e.g., verbal fluency).
C−A (uncovered maze vs motor control) is a within-group whole-brain contrast of a maze-processing task that involves visuospatial memory/rehearsal and attentional/executive demands.

Although uncovered maze traversal involves visuospatial processing and rehearsal, the contrast and authors' interpretation emphasize posterior/episodic/visual imagery regions rather than canonical short-term working-memory maintenance manipulations; it does not meet WORKING_MEMORY_I1.

Passive View > Remember Scenes is a within-group, whole-brain task contrast derived from the same WM paradigm and thus falls within the pooled executive domains.

REV (response reversal) clearly taps executive-function processes (requires inhibiting the learned/prepotent response and switching to a new rule), so it falls within the set of six EF domains. REV is not a canonical working-memory paradigm (no n-back/Sternberg/DMTS load manipulation). Missing: WORKING_MEMORY_I1.
Response reversal requires inhibiting the previously learned/prepotent response in order to make the less-prepotent (correct) response, meeting the inhibition-domain definition.
Response reversal requires switching the stimulus–response mapping/rule and thus corresponds to set-shifting/cognitive flexibility as defined.
REV does not constitute a Tower-type planning task. Missing: PLANNING_I1.
REV is not an oddball/vigilance sustained target-detection paradigm. Missing: VIGILANCE_I1.
REV is not a word-generation/self-initiation paradigm. Missing: INITIATION_I1.
